questions.q: In one hybrid training iteration, which steps happen on the quantum side versus the classical side?
options: Quantum: running the circuit (including shifted evaluations for gradients) to get expectation values. Classical: loss computation, gradient assembly, and the optimizer update
Quantum: computing the loss function. Classical: running the circuit and measuring observables
Everything happens entirely on the quantum device, with no classical computation anywhere
Everything happens entirely on the classical computer, with the quantum circuit used only for display purposes
questions.explain: The circuit (at current and shifted parameters) runs on the quantum side producing numbers; loss computation, gradient assembly from those shifted evaluations, and the optimizer's parameter update are all classical arithmetic on a classical computer.

questions.q: Why can't the entire training loop (including the optimizer) run on quantum hardware with zero classical computation, per this lesson?
options: There is no known way to run gradient aggregation and optimizer state updates (e.g., Adam's running averages) as a quantum circuit -- that arithmetic is done classically because only classical hardware currently does it efficiently
Quantum hardware is physically incapable of storing any numbers at all
Classical computers are not allowed to communicate with quantum devices under current protocols
The parameter-shift rule can only be computed on a classical computer, never on real quantum hardware
questions.explain: Optimizer logic (gradient descent, Adam's moving averages, etc.) is ordinary classical arithmetic with no known quantum-circuit implementation, which is exactly why every practical QML training approach today is hybrid, not purely quantum.

questions.q: For a circuit with k trainable parameters using the parameter-shift rule, how many quantum-side circuit evaluations does ONE full gradient step require, before any classical-side computation?
options: 2k evaluations (two shifted evaluations per parameter)
k evaluations total
1 evaluation regardless of k
k^2 evaluations
questions.explain: As established in Lesson 7, each parameter needs a plus-shift and minus-shift evaluation, giving 2k total quantum-side circuit evaluations before the classical side assembles and applies the gradient.

questions.q: What specific real-world cost does the lesson point to as a reason variational model training can take much longer in wall-clock time than a comparable classical model's training?
options: Round-trip overhead between classical host and quantum device, plus queueing time behind other users' jobs on shared cloud quantum hardware
Quantum circuits always have more trainable parameters than any classical model of comparable size
Classical GPUs cannot run any kind of gradient descent, unlike quantum hardware
There is no such cost; quantum training is always faster in wall-clock time
questions.explain: Every classical-to-quantum-and-back round trip costs real time, and on shared cloud quantum hardware there's additional queueing time behind other users -- costs that don't exist for a purely classical model trained on local or cloud GPUs.

questions.q: A colleague claims 'we're building a fully quantum ML pipeline with no classical computation anywhere in the loop.' Based on this lesson, how should you evaluate that claim?
options: It is not accurate for any currently practiced QML approach -- the optimizer's gradient aggregation and parameter updates are always ordinary classical computation, even when the circuit itself runs on quantum hardware
The claim is accurate and describes the current state of all practical QML systems
The claim can only be evaluated by running the pipeline, since no general answer exists
The claim is accurate as long as the circuit uses more than 50 qubits
questions.explain: Every current practical QML training approach relies on classical computation for the optimizer loop; a genuinely 'fully quantum, zero classical computation' training pipeline does not exist today, which is exactly why this course calls these systems 'hybrid.'
